title: Saudi Coalition Bombs Sanaa's Fuel Depot as the Houthis Vow a 'Painful' Reply, and Russia Hits Kyiv's Power Grid With No Allied Warning
subhead: Two escalations moved sharply forward overnight — Saudi Arabia struck a major oil facility in Yemen's capital and the Houthis hit an Aramco compound in the kingdom's Eastern Province, while Russian ballistic missiles knocked out a key Kyiv power plant that Ukraine's partners never warned it about.

sections.heading: Sanaa Fuel Depot Hit as the Saudi-Houthi War Widens
sections.body:
The Saudi-led coalition struck the Al-Sahaba oil facility near Sanaa on Tuesday after warning civilians away from the site, according to AFP (via Dawn) and Al-Monitor. Houthi-run media reported explosions across the capital, and the group's leadership vowed what it called a 'painful response' inside Saudi Arabia. The exchange was not one-sided: Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said a limited fire broke out in an administrative building at an Aramco facility in the Eastern Province, per AP, after the Houthis claimed to have targeted the site.

AP reports the coalition framed the Sanaa strike as an operation to 'cut off vital supply sources' used by the Houthis. The Houthi-run Yemen Petroleum Company insisted Sanaa had sufficient fuel stocks — a claim that signals how central the depot is to both the group's logistics and the capital's civilian supply. The Houthis have staged armed rallies in Sanaa against the involvement of Türkiye and Pakistan alongside Saudi Arabia, according to Xinhua.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first time in the current escalation that the two sides have struck each other's core energy assets within a single day — Sanaa's main fuel hub and an Aramco site in the Saudi oil heartland. Targeting Aramco directly raises the cost for Riyadh and pulls the world's largest crude exporter's own infrastructure into the line of fire.

sections.heading: Kyiv's Power Plant Struck Without Warning From Allies
sections.body:
Russian ballistic missiles hit a key thermal power plant and an apartment building in Kyiv, killing two people, according to Reuters (via BBC), Euronews and India Today. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no early warning from its partners ahead of the strike — a claim carried by Ukrainska Pravda, Ukrinform, RBC-Ukraine, NBC News and Anadolu. Ukrinform reports the strike involved five ballistic missiles; Zelenskyy called the absence of advance intelligence 'absolutely unjust.'

The timing is awkward for Washington: Zelenskyy said Russia is ignoring the US-brokered energy ceasefire, noting Ukraine had not struck Russian oil or energy sites in the two days prior, per NBC News. The strike came on a second consecutive day of Russian ballistic attacks on Kyiv with no advance warning, per Al Jazeera.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's air-defence problem is now also an intelligence-sharing problem. If allies are not passing ballistic-launch warnings to Kyiv, the credibility of the wider US-brokered de-escalation framework weakens — and Russia's winter campaign against the grid can proceed with less friction.

sections.heading: US and Saudi Arabia Sign 30-Year Civil Nuclear Agreement
sections.body:
The US Department of Energy announced a civil nuclear cooperation agreement signed by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman. AP reports the agreement runs 30 years and could potentially provide the kingdom with uranium enrichment capability — the central proliferation question in the deal. It is a Section 123 agreement; the earlier presidential determination was published in the Federal Register on 28 July.

The deal is not settled: the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists argues Congress retains the power to amend its terms, and the congressional review window is now the key battleground over whether enrichment goes ahead or is constrained by a 'gold standard' of inspections.
sections.whyItMatters: A US blessing for Saudi enrichment would reshape the Middle East's nuclear balance at the same moment Iran's programme is under maximum pressure — and it hands Congress a rare lever over a signature Trump foreign-policy deal.

sections.heading: South Korea's First Hypersonic Glide Vehicle Test
sections.body:
South Korea conducted the first test launch of a domestically developed hypersonic glide vehicle, with President Lee Jae-myung observing, according to Yonhap, the Korea Herald and the presidential office briefing. Seoul's Yonhap reported the vehicle flies more than twice as fast as conventional supersonic jets. Lee framed the test around 'self-reliant defence,' per the Hankyoreh, and called it 'a new means of deterrence,' per SBS.

The test lands amid continued North Korean missile activity and follows Seoul's earlier signals on naval modernization. It places South Korea in a small club of states fielding or testing hypersonic glide technology, alongside the US, China, Russia and North Korea.
sections.whyItMatters: A hypersonic capability inside a treaty ally changes the balance on the Korean Peninsula and in the wider Pacific. It also deepens Seoul's push for defence autonomy at a moment when Washington's regional force posture is stretched by the Iran war.

sections.heading: Pakistan Entrenches Emergency Rule in Imran Khan's Stronghold
sections.body:
Pakistan's federal government imposed emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the PTI stronghold, after President Asif Ali Zardari approved the cabinet decision, per Dawn. Police placed provincial assembly speaker Sohail Afridi and other KP ministers in 'preventive custody,' Dawn and Al-Monitor report. The Indian Express described the move as a 'coup disguised as emergency'; NPR and CNA note the government cites a rise in militant attacks.

Legal bodies have pushed back: Dawn reports the legal fraternity railed against the proclamation, and the BBC notes the lockdown of Khan's political base could 'backfire.' The PTI's provincial government has effectively been suspended.
sections.whyItMatters: Suspending an elected provincial government in a nuclear-armed state is a significant break, but the deeper risk is security: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa borders Afghanistan, and removing civilian governance there while militancy rises is a governance vacuum, not a solution.

sections.heading: Ethiopia and Eritrea Edge Toward Direct War
sections.body:
The International Crisis Group warned on 12 October that Addis Ababa and Asmara are 'edging closer to a direct conflict.' BBC Tigrinya reported Eritrean troops moving deep into Ethiopia's Tigray region, and Reuters (via Mereja) reported Ethiopian forces entering the border town of Adigrat as Eritrea asked the UN Security Council to condemn what it called a 'declaration of war.' Ethiopia formally accused Eritrea of an invasion reaching up to 60km, per the Field reporters.

The two countries were allies as recently as the 2020-22 Tigray war, which makes the reversal sharp. Residents' accounts of troop movements remain the primary evidence, and both capitals dispute the other's version.
sections.whyItMatters: A new Ethiopia-Eritrea war would be the Horn of Africa's most destabilizing conflict in a decade, reopening the Red Sea's western flank at a time when the waterway's eastern side is already a war zone.

bottomLine: The day's pattern is escalation on multiple fronts rather than any single de-escalation. Saudi Arabia and the Houthis traded strikes on each other's energy infrastructure — a first for this round — while Russia hit Kyiv's power grid without the allied warning that underpins the US-brokered energy truce. In parallel, Washington deepened its Middle East alignment with a 30-year Saudi nuclear deal whose enrichment terms Congress can still fight over, Seoul crossed a hypersonic threshold, and both Pakistan and the Horn of Africa slid further from stable governance. The common thread is that several of the world's most fragile theaters are hardening at once, and the outside powers best positioned to restrain them are either distracted or, in Kyiv's case, not sharing what they know.
